narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 66.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that mattered most to this decision were, in order of importance, your LSAT score, your class ranking in the third year of law school, and your class ranking in the first year. Your LSAT score was the strongest positive influence, pushing the prediction toward passing because you scored 38—slightly above the average of students who were accepted. Unfortunately, this helpful effect was more than offset by the other two factors.

Your third-year class ranking of 2.0 placed you far below the average ranking of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this low standing strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Similarly, your first-year ranking of 2.0—well below the accepted-student average of 6.0—also pulled the prediction in the failure direction, though less forcefully than the third-year ranking.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively modest academic standing in law school outweighed the benefit of your solid LSAT performance, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses or seeking targeted tutoring in the areas where your class performance lagged. Improving those rankings in future semesters or through supplemental study could meaningfully change your outlook for re-application. (218 words)
